chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Muhammad, from Yunus, from a number (of people), from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
A man said to him: 'May I be sacrificed for you! Did God compel the servants to commit sins?' He said: 'God is too just to compel them to commit sins and then punish them for it.'

So he said to him: 'May I be sacrificed for you! So did God delegate (the choice) to the servants?' (The narrator) said, so he said: 'If He had delegated to them, He would not have confined them with commands and prohibitions.'
So he said to him: 'May I be sacrificed for you! So there is a (third) status between the two?' (The narrator) said, so he said: 'Yes, more extensive than what is between the sky and the earth.'

key_terms.أَعْدَلُ: more just — divine justice (ʿadl) as the theological ground for rejecting compulsion
key_terms.الْمَعَاصِي: sins/disobediences — acts of defiance against divine commands, the crux of the jabr debate
key_terms.فَوَّضَ: delegated — tafwid: the doctrine of absolute human autonomy, rejected here
key_terms.مَنْزِلَةٌ: station/position — the middle way between jabr and tafwid; al-amr bayna al-amrayn
key_terms.يَحْصُرْهُمْ: to confine/surround — divine commands and prohibitions prove humans have real but bounded agency

ai.seo_question: What does Imam al-Sadiq (AS) teach about divine compulsion (jabr), human free will (tafwid), and the doctrine of al-amr bayna al-amrayn?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) systematically dismantles two theological extremes put to him by a questioner: jabr (God compels humans to sin) and tafwid (God surrenders all agency entirely to humans). Jabr is refuted via divine justice — a just God cannot compel then punish for the same act; tafwid is refuted via the very existence of divine commands and prohibitions, which would be absurd if humans had no real but also no divinely-bounded agency. The resulting middle doctrine, al-amr bayna al-amrayn, is declared vaster than the space between sky and earth.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from Muhammad, from Yunus, from a number (of people), 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>, said,

‘A man said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘May I be sacrificed for you<sup>asws</sup>! Does Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Compel the servants upon the disobedience?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Allah<sup>azwj</sup> is more Just that for Him<sup>azwj</sup> to Compel them upon the disobedience then Punishing them upon it’.

So he said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘May I be sacrificed for you<sup>asws</sup>! So does Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Delegate to the servants?’ So He<sup>azwj</sup> Said: ‘If He<sup>azwj</sup> had Delegated to them, He<sup>azwj</sup> would not have Surrounded them with the Commands and the Prohibitions’.

So he said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘May I be sacrificed for you<sup>asws</sup>! So there is a (third) status between the two?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘Yes, more extensive than what is between the sky and the earth’.
